entities.name: Titus Cloelius Siculus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Titus Cloelius Siculus, a distinguished patrician of the Roman Republic, held the pivotal role of one of the inaugural consular tribunes in 444 BCE, a critical period marking the nascent stages of Rome's republican governance. His brief tenure illuminates the volatile political landscape of the mid-5th century BCE, characterized by intense patrician-plebeian struggles and the experimental evolution of executive magistracies. As a figure whose public service was abruptly terminated by a religious technicality, his story underscores the profound influence of augury and ritual on Roman political legitimacy, even as new governmental forms were being forged.

Elected to the newly instituted consular tribunate in 444 BCE alongside Lucius Atilius Luscus and Aulus Sempronius Atratinus, Siculus found his magistracy invalidated shortly after assuming office. The traditional accounts, notably by Livy, attribute this annulment to a procedural flaw (vitium) discovered by the augurs during his election, specifically an imperfection in the taking of the auspices. This religious decree compelled the entire college of consular tribunes to abdicate, leading to the swift election of suffect consuls. Two years later, in 442 BCE, Siculus re-emerged in public life as one of the triumviri coloniae deducendae, the three commissioners appointed to establish a Roman colony at Ardea, a strategic settlement approximately 35 kilometers south of Rome, following a dispute over its territory with the Aequi.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Titus Cloelius Siculus's short-lived consular tribunate provides a concrete example of the early Roman Republic's political instability and the enduring power of religious authority over nascent institutions. His experience contributed to the ongoing evolution and eventual stabilization of Roman executive magistracies.
